strand: Methods v3: how comparable studies handled five weaknesses of the 86-winter model: (1) thermal mass and pre-heating, (2) price response and herding, (3) realistic housing stock, (4) capital and gas-network costs, (5) multiple price years; plus the most comparable published national heat-electrification models
method_note: Every source below was found by web search and then downloaded on 2026-11-07 (curl) and read via pdftotext or HTML text extraction; quotes were machine-checked against the downloaded text (token order, ligatures and two-column interleaving tolerated). 'PDF p.' is the page index of the downloaded file. Where a repository copy (arXiv, accepted manuscript, working paper) was read instead of the publisher version, the Harvard entry says so and numbers are those of the copy read. Figures marked 'derived' are this reviewer's arithmetic, not the source's. Two data probes were also run on 2026-11-07 and are reported, not quoted: the NESO N2EX day-ahead CSV holds hourly prices from 2021-09-20 to 2026-11-08 (45,001 rows); the Elexon Insights API returned market-index (APX/N2EX MID) half-hourly prices from a date between 2016-09-10 and 2016-11-10 onward, and system prices for 2016-01-07 but not 2015-01-07. Sources already in hybrid_peak.json or controls_flex.json (Watson 2019/2021, Love 2017, Freedom, Pean 2019, Strbac 2018, Carbon Trust 2016) are not re-quoted except where a different claim is used.

claims.claim: Open hourly heat and COP series built for weather-year sensitivity (later releases extend the years).
claims.quote: Furthermore, eleven years (2008–2018) are included to enable weather year sensitivity analyses.

claims.claim: Openness.
claims.quote: The dataset, as well as the scripts and input parameters, are publicly available under an open source license on the Open Power System Data platform.
